Stonehenge. A monumental circle of standing stones on the Salisbury Plain in England, built in stages over more than fifteen hundred years, from roughly 3100 to 1500 BCE. Its massive sarsen stones arranged in precise astronomical alignments, combined with evidence of ritual gatherings and burials, suggest it served as a temple, ceremonial calendar, or sacred meeting place, though its exact purpose remains debated and mysterious.

Located on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England, Stonehenge was built in multiple phases over the Neolithic and Bronze Age periods. The outer circle consists of thirty sarsen stones—a type of sandstone—weighing up to twenty-five tons each, quarried from the Marlborough Downs twenty miles away. An inner circle of sixty smaller bluestones, composed of dolerite, was transported from the Preseli Mountains in Wales, a distance of one hundred fifty miles, representing an extraordinary logistical feat for prehistoric people.

The monument is oriented to align with the winter and summer solstices. The sun rises over the Heel Stone at the summer solstice sunrise, a precise astronomical alignment that suggests sophisticated understanding of celestial cycles. Archaeological excavations reveal cremated bones of thousands of individuals buried at the site, indicating it served as a burial place and a gathering site for ritual ceremonies.

The name Stonehenge derives from Old English, but its original purpose remains unknown, with theories ranging from an astronomical observatory to a healing temple to a ceremonial calendar. Built by Neolithic and Bronze Age societies with no written language, Stonehenge represents knowledge preserved through oral tradition and transmitted by specialized craftspeople. It remains one of England's most famous prehistoric monuments and central to British archaeological heritage.
